title: A heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26)
hook: I will take out the heart of stone

segments.voice: Yesterday, the valley of dry bones, and your line was can these bones live? What stalled thing got a breath? Day four hundred seventy-nine.

Stone doesn't feel anything. That's what makes it good for walls. A sibling, an old friend, a parent, a coworker: someone hurts a person enough times, and something in that person goes hard. The name pops up on a phone, and there's nothing, or worse, a kind of cold click. It works like protection, and sometimes it is. But walls have a way of spreading: harder with one person, then a little harder with everyone. Ezekiel had a word for that. He'd watched a whole people grow hard: hard toward God, hard toward the poor, hard toward the truth. Today, a promise about the heart.
screen: `A NAME POPS UP.` → `A COLD CLICK.` → `THE HARDNESS SPREADS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, God says through Ezekiel: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh." First, the heart. In the Hebrew Bible, the heart, lev, isn't mainly where you feel. It's often where people think, decide and choose. Your whole inner self. So a heart of stone isn't just sadness. It's a self that can't be moved, can't be taught, can't respond. And a heart of flesh is one that's alive again: soft enough to feel, to change, to care. Notice the trade isn't weak for strong. It's stone for flesh. Flesh can be hurt. That's the point. Only something that can be hurt can also love. Now look back a few chapters. Earlier in the same book, in chapter eighteen, Ezekiel tells the people: make you a new heart and a new spirit. Make it yourselves. And here in thirty-six, God says: I will give you a new heart. So which is it? The book holds both. Some readers put it this way: the new heart is something you're called to reach for, and something you can only receive. Christians often connect this verse to the work of the Holy Spirit, and Jewish readers hear in it God's promise to renew Israel after exile. Both hear the same image: stone, taken out; flesh, given back.
screen: `A NEW HEART WILL I GIVE YOU.` · `LEV: WHERE YOU THINK AND CHOOSE.` · `ONLY FLESH CAN BE HURT, OR LOVE.` · `MAKE IT, OR RECEIVE IT? BOTH.` · then, large: `AN HEART OF FLESH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften toward one person, just a little. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've gone hard toward. Not the person who hurt you most; start smaller. Picture their face. Notice the stone: the tight chest, the set jaw, the ready list of what they did. Don't throw the list away. Just set it down for a minute. Then try to see one ordinary, human thing about them: they get tired, they were a child once, someone they love is sick. Let your chest loosen by one degree. If you pray, you can ask for a heart of flesh. The bell holds the time.
Lev. The Hebrew word for heart, meaning the whole inner self: where you think, decide and choose, not only where you feel.
Your line: loosen by one degree. Today, soften toward one person: a kinder word, a reply you'd usually skip, or simply not adding to the list. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Christians often pray Ezekiel 36:26 when asking God to change them, and it is read at the Easter Vigil, at confirmations and at services of renewal; it appears in many hymns and worship songs about the Spirit.

fork.reveal: Ezekiel 18:31 says make you a new heart; 36:26 says a new heart also will I give you. the book holds both.

original.note: Hebrew: a heart of flesh. lev means the whole inner self.

trapdoor: what you thought: a heart of flesh means becoming more emotional.
what it means: a hard, unresponsive self replaced with a living one that can feel, change and love.
what a scholar hears: lev covers mind and will as well as feeling. the promise echoes Ezekiel 11:19 and pairs with 18:31, where the people are told to make a new heart themselves.
